fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Caleb says, "…I remained loyal to the LORD my God." Right before that, he says his brothers who went with him made the hearts of the people melt with fear. Joshua 14:8 sets those two things side by side, and Caleb puts himself on the loyal side. That's a line worth hanging onto.

Not quite, friend. Caleb never says he stayed quiet. He says Moses sent him to spy out the land and he brought "…an honest report." (Joshua 14:7). Then he says, "…I remained loyal to the LORD my God." (Joshua 14:8). I think quiet would have been the easy road, but that's not the road he describes.

A second spy trip would mean a lot more walking, baker, but Caleb doesn't mention one. He says Moses sent him to spy out the land and he brought back "…an honest report." (Joshua 14:7). What he says he did next is "…I remained loyal to the LORD my God." (Joshua 14:8). Loyalty is his claim, not a return visit.

Close, but this passage mentions no battle for them. Joshua 14:3 says Moses had given the inheritance east of the Jordan to the other two and a half tribes. So the lot only had to cover the nine and a half. The text gives Moses' gift as the reason, friend, and nothing about a fight.

Tents is a fair guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. Joshua 14:4 says the Levites got "…cities in which to live, along with pasturelands for their flocks and herds." So the text gives them cities, plus pasturelands for their animals. No tent shows up on that list.

Caves, huh? I spent years in the back of a dark, dusty junk drawer, so I get the pull of a hideaway. But Joshua 14:4 says the Levites got cities to live in, plus pasturelands for their flocks and herds. No caves on that list, baker.

That's right. Moses swore, "…the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God." (Joshua 14:9). Notice the reason Moses gives, baker. Caleb had wholly followed the LORD, and the promise was attached to the ground under his feet.

The Jordan is a reasonable guess, friend, but the verse doesn't point to a river at all. Moses swore, "…the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever…" (Joshua 14:9). The land is named by where Caleb had set foot. That's the detail to hold onto.

Gilgal is where the sons of Judah approach Joshua (Joshua 14:6), so I see the pull, baker. But Moses' oath doesn't name Gilgal. He swore, "…the land on which you have set foot will be an inheritance to you and your children forever…" (Joshua 14:9). The promise points to where Caleb had set foot.

Ninety overshoots by five, baker. Forty plus forty-five is eighty-five, and Caleb says it himself: "…here I am today, eighty-five years old…" (Joshua 14:10). Your math was running a little hot there, friend. Pull it out of the oven and count again.

Right, baker. Caleb says, "Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken." Just before, he tells Joshua he's still strong for war (Joshua 14:11). He also names the Anakim's great and fortified cities. And when he talks about driving them out, he names the LORD's help.

Amorites is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the name in this verse. It says Kiriath-arba was named "…after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim." (Joshua 14:15). The Anakim are the people Caleb mentions back in verse 12, with their great and fortified cities.

Philistines is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the name in this verse. It says Kiriath-arba was named "…after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim." (Joshua 14:15). Caleb mentions the Anakim in verse 12, along with their great and fortified cities.
